terms.gloss: himself (as object), referring to the subject
terms.grammar: pronoun, reflexive: genitive suī, dative sibi, accusative and ablative sē; the same for every gender and number
evidence: Publ. B 21: Bis vincit quī sē vincit in victōriā.
terms.comment: The reflexive refers to the subject of its clause: quī sē vincit, who masters himself. It has no nominative. “With himself” is sēcum. In reported speech it stands for the speaker: cujātem sē esse dīceret, where he would say he (himself) was from.

terms.gloss: himself (for emphasis: he himself, in person, of his own accord)
terms.grammar: pronoun, intensive: genitive ipsīus, dative ipsī
evidence: Publ. Q 69: Quī sē ipse laudat, citō dērīsōrem invenit.
terms.comment: Stresses the person: ipse Hannibal, Hannibal himself. With the reflexive it agrees with the subject when it stresses the doer, quī sē ipse laudat, who praises himself (no one else praises him); with the object when it stresses the object, sē ipsum fēlīcem facit (Lewis & Short, s.v. ipse).

phrases.latin: Bis vincit quī sē vincit in victōriā.
phrases.english: He wins twice who masters himself in victory.

phrases.latin: Īrātus, cum ad sē rediit, sibi tum īrāscitur.
phrases.english: The angry man, when he comes back to himself, is then angry with himself.

phrases.latin: Quī sē ipse laudat, citō dērīsōrem invenit.
phrases.english: Whoever praises himself soon finds someone to laugh at him.

phrases.latin: Patiēns et fortis sē ipsum fēlīcem facit.
phrases.english: The patient and brave man makes himself happy.

phrases.latin: locō herbidō ut quiēte et pābulō laetō reficeret bovēs et ipsum fessum viā prōcubuisse
phrases.english: in a grassy spot, to rest his cattle with quiet and rich pasture, and that he himself, tired from the road, lay down

phrases.latin: sēcum esse sēcumque, ut dīcitur, vīvere
phrases.english: to be with oneself and, as they say, to live with oneself
